To understand "derisory," you first need to know one word: derision.

Derision means mockery — the act of laughing at something or someone because you think they are foolish, pathetic, or not worthy of being taken seriously. Think of the way a crowd might laugh and jeer at a terrible performance. That laughter is derision.

Now, derisory is the adjective built from that idea. Something described as "derisory" is so bad, so small, or so ridiculous that it invites that kind of mocking laughter. It is laughably poor. It doesn't just fall short — it falls so far short that people scoff at it.

"Derisory" carries two closely related meanings, and both flow naturally from the same core idea.

Sense 1 — Ridiculously Small or Inadequate (the most common use)

This is the sense you will encounter most often in everyday writing and speech.

When something is described as "derisory," it means it is so laughably insufficient — so far below what is reasonable or expected — that the only appropriate reaction is to scoff at it.

The key feeling here is insult through inadequacy. The thing being described is not just small — it is small to the point of being an embarrassment, almost an insult to the person receiving it.

Examples:

  • "The workers demanded a 10% pay rise, but the company offered a derisory 0.5%."

Here, the offer is so tiny compared to what was asked that it's almost a joke. People would laugh at how poor it is.

  • "The charity raised millions, but the government's contribution was a derisory £500."

Five hundred pounds from a government is so little it's almost offensive. It invites mockery.

  • "He sold his painting for a derisory sum — barely enough to cover the cost of the canvas."

The amount is absurdly small given the effort involved.

Notice the pattern: "derisory" is very commonly used before words like offer, sum, amount, pay rise, wage, figure, fee. Whenever something measurable — money, time, effort — falls shockingly below a fair or expected standard, "derisory" is the right word.

Sense 2 — Expressing Mockery or Scorn

Less commonly, "derisory" can also describe something that contains or expresses mockery — a tone, a laugh, a comment that ridicules something or someone.

Examples:

  • "She gave a derisory laugh when he claimed he could run a marathon."

The laugh itself is the mockery. It communicates: "That's ridiculous."

  • "His derisory tone made it clear he had no respect for their opinion."

The tone drips with contempt and ridicule.

In this sense, "derisory" overlaps with another word — derisive — which only carries this mocking meaning. In modern English, "derisive" has become the preferred word for this sense (mocking tone, mocking laughter), while "derisory" has become the dominant word for Sense 1 (laughably inadequate). That said, "derisory" in the mocking sense is not wrong — it is simply less common today.

This is important: "derisory" is not a neutral word. It carries strong negative judgment.

When a journalist writes that a government's climate pledge is "derisory," they are not merely saying it is small. They are saying it is insultingly small — so small that serious people cannot take it seriously. The word conveys both factual inadequacy and emotional contempt for that inadequacy.

This makes "derisory" a powerful word. It does two things at once: it states that something falls short, and it implies that any reasonable person would find that shameful or ridiculous.
"Derisory" vs. Words You Might Confuse It With

Derisory vs. Derisive

  • Derisive = expressing mockery. A derisive comment makes fun of something.
  • Derisory = either worthy of mockery (laughably small) or expressing mockery.
  • Rule of thumb: use derisive for a mocking person or tone; use derisory for an offer, amount, or figure that is embarrassingly inadequate.

Derisory vs. Paltry / Meagre / Negligible
These words also describe things that are very small, but they are softer and more neutral. They simply mean "not much." Derisory goes further — it adds the layer of contempt. A "meagre salary" is just small. A "derisory salary" is so small it's almost laughable.

Derisory vs. Insulting
Something "insulting" deliberately disrespects you. Something "derisory" may not be deliberate — it may simply be so poor that it feels like an insult. The word focuses on the reaction of ridicule rather than on intent.

Whenever you see or hear "derisory," ask yourself: "Is this so bad/small/inadequate that a sensible person would laugh at it?" If the answer is yes, that's "derisory."

Imagine someone working 60 hours a week and being offered a £1 bonus. That bonus is derisory. The word captures not just the smallness of the amount, but the almost comical gap between what was deserved and what was given.
